strengths: Identifies and formalizes a novel and practically relevant failure mode, 'multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing', distinguishing it clearly from single-agent hallucination and from prior textual hallucination snowballing work.

Provides an extensive multi-level (turn-, layer-, token-wise) attention analysis that builds a coherent empirical narrative for why hallucinations propagate in MAS, and replicates these analyses across six different VLMs in the appendix to support generality.

The identification of a specific 'unimodal attention peak' vision-token subset in middle layers, validated through careful token-dropping ablations (random/inactive/rise/fall/unimodal), is a nice piece of diagnostic evidence that directly motivates the proposed method.

Very comprehensive experimental evaluation: 10 base VLMs (7B-34B), 4 MAS topologies, 8 benchmarks (comprehensive + hallucination-specific), plus scaling experiments on larger models (32B/34B) showing consistent, non-trivial gains.

Introduces a new hallucination-snowballing metric (HS) to explicitly quantify propagation severity, and shows that existing single-agent hallucination mitigation methods (MemVR, VISTA, FarSight, DeCo, TAME) actually underperform in MAS settings, which is an interesting and somewhat counterintuitive finding that strengthens the paper's motivation.

Practical engineering consideration for real deployment: an attention-score-free alternative (Key-Norm) for models using Flash-Attention where attention weights are inaccessible, with an ablation showing near-parity performance.
Thorough ablation and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (ω, τ, α1, α2) supporting the design choices.
weaknesses: The method is advertised as 'lightweight, plug-and-play' but actually requires a two-stage training pipeline (pre-training + instruction tuning) with a trainable transformer block and partial LLM fine-tuning, which is a meaningful practical cost that somewhat undercuts the plug-and-play framing; details on training data, size, and compute cost are largely absent from the main text.

The construction of 'agent turns' in the evaluation setup is not clearly justified as representative of realistic multi-agent tasks; it appears turns are simulated by repeatedly querying the same static image with a chain of questions, which may not faithfully capture the dynamics of genuine collaborative MAS pipelines (e.g., planning, tool use, heterogeneous roles) noted in related MAS literature (Cemri et al., 2025).

The proposed HS metric (Equation 7) is somewhat ad hoc (sigmoid-weighted average hallucination severity over propagation distance) without independent validation against human judgments of snowballing severity, and no inter-annotator or correlation analysis is provided to justify its reliability as a snowballing indicator.

Token subset selection procedures (rise/fall/unimodal/inactive) rely on multiple hand-tuned thresholds (tolerance thresholds, quartiles, salience ω) whose sensitivity and robustness across tasks/domains beyond the tested benchmarks is not deeply explored.

No variance/statistical significance reporting across multiple runs or random seeds, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements (often 1-3 points) are robust rather than noise, especially given the many benchmarks/structures/models compared.

Limited discussion of computational overhead (extra transformer block, additional visual relay tokens, attention reallocation) relative to baselines and existing methods in terms of latency/memory, despite this being important for a method emphasizing efficiency.

The comparison to prior work is restricted to single-agent hallucination mitigation baselines; no comparison to any other genuinely multi-agent-oriented mitigation strategy (if any exist) or to simple non-visual baselines (e.g., re-supplying the raw image to every agent) that might already alleviate part of the observed degradation.

strengths: Identifies and clearly formalizes a novel and important failure mode specific to VLM-based multi-agent systems (visual hallucination snowballing), distinguishing it conceptually from prior single-agent hallucination-snowballing work.

Conducts thorough, multi-faceted diagnostic analyses (turn-wise, layer-wise, and token-wise attention) that build a coherent and largely convincing causal narrative for why hallucinations compound across agent turns, with the unimodal-token ablation study providing good supporting evidence.

Very broad empirical validation: 8 benchmarks (comprehensive + hallucination-specific), 10 base VLMs spanning 7B-34B, and 4 different MAS topologies, with consistent improvements across nearly all settings.

Provides a sensible Key-Norm-based alternative for attention-score-dependent token selection, making the method compatible with Flash-Attention-based models where raw attention scores are unavailable.

Introduces a dedicated hallucination-snowballing (HS) metric and demonstrates via comparisons with five recent single-agent hallucination-mitigation methods that those approaches fail (and sometimes worsen results) in MAS settings, strengthening the paper's core claim that propagation, not just intrinsic hallucination, must be addressed.
Appendix contains generalization checks across six VLMs for the core attention analyses and hyperparameter sensitivity studies, adding confidence to the robustness of the findings.
weaknesses: The method is described as 'lightweight, plug-and-play' throughout, but Appendix D.1/Table 8 reveals a two-stage training pipeline (pre-training + instruction tuning) for the added transformer block and partial LLM fine-tuning; this conflicts with the plug-and-play framing and raises reproducibility/cost concerns, since training data and compute budget for this stage are not clearly specified.

The proposed HS metric (Eq. 7) relies on an unspecified 'judge model' scoring hallucination severity and an ad hoc sigmoid-of-distance weighting scheme; the design choices are not theoretically justified or validated against human judgments, making the metric's reliability somewhat uncertain.

No variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-run statistics are reported for any experiment; given that some absolute gains are modest (2-4% average), it is hard to assess statistical significance of the improvements.

Key hyperparameters (ω, τ, α1, α2) appear to be tuned on a single model/MAS-structure combination (LLaVA-NeXT-7B, circular) and then applied uniformly across all other experiments; the generalizability of this fixed configuration to very different models/structures is asserted but not rigorously justified.

No analysis of computational/memory overhead (extra transformer block, additional relay tokens, attention reallocation) relative to baseline MAS communication, which is important for a method motivated partly by efficiency/lightweightness.

The approach presumes access to internal representations (vision tokens, attention scores or key vectors) of every agent, which may not generalize to heterogeneous MAS with closed-source or architecturally different VLM agents; this limitation is not discussed.

Related-work differentiation from Zhong et al. (2024), the closest prior work on multimodal hallucination snowballing, remains largely qualitative in the introduction without a deeper empirical or technical comparison in the main experiments.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes a novel and practically relevant failure mode—multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing—that is distinct from single-agent hallucination and single-model hallucination snowballing studied in prior work.

Provides a detailed multi-level (turn-, layer-, token-wise) attention analysis that motivates the method, including a systematic ablation of five different token subsets (random, inactive, rise, fall, unimodal) across shallow/middle/deep layers, which convincingly shows that a specific 'unimodal' subset of vision tokens is disproportionately important.

The proposed ViF method (visual relay tokens + attention reallocation) is lightweight, model-agnostic, and includes a practical fallback (Key-Norm) for models using FlashAttention where attention scores are unavailable.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 10 base VLMs (7B-34B), 4 MAS structures, 8 main benchmarks plus 4 augmented multi-image/video benchmarks, comparison against 5 recent single-agent hallucination mitigation baselines, ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, efficiency/latency analysis, and case studies.

Introduces a new hallucination-snowballing (HS) metric that attempts to jointly capture severity and propagation distance, providing a more targeted way to measure the phenomenon beyond standard benchmark scores.

Shows that existing single-agent hallucination mitigation methods can actually underperform the baseline in MAS settings, which is an interesting and non-trivial empirical finding that supports the paper's core thesis.
weaknesses: The construction of the 'multi-agent' evaluation setting itself (how single-turn benchmarks like MME, POPE, CHAIR are converted into 1-20 turn agent pipelines, what task/question each agent receives, how ground truth propagates) is underspecified in the main text and only loosely covered in the appendix, which is critical for judging the validity and realism of the reported hallucination snowballing curves.

The proposed HS metric is defined by the authors themselves and evaluated using an LLM-as-judge (a specific GPT-5 checkpoint) with a custom prompt; since this same metric is then used to show the method's largest relative gains (30-40% reduction), there is a risk of metric/judge bias favoring the proposed approach, and reproducibility of exact judge behavior is questionable given reliance on a closed, versioned model.

The causal link between reduced attention to 'unimodal' vision tokens and downstream hallucination snowballing is established mainly via correlational analyses (attention allocation trends, token-dropping ablations in a single-turn setting) rather than a controlled causal intervention within the actual multi-turn MAS pipeline, leaving open whether the identified token subset is the true driver of snowballing versus a correlate.

Reported improvements are numerically small and strikingly uniform (roughly +2-4% average) across nearly all 10 models, 4 structures, and most benchmarks, which is good for demonstrating robustness but also raises questions about whether some benchmarks/metrics were selectively reported or whether gains are within noise for certain tasks (e.g., CHAIR occasionally worsens slightly).

The method requires an additional trained lightweight transformer block and a two-stage training pipeline (pretraining + instruction tuning) per base model, which is not fully 'training-free' as implied by comparisons to some training-free baselines, complicating fair comparison and practical deployment.

Limited engagement with why the same phenomenon could not be explained/mitigated by simply increasing textual grounding or re-summarizing images between agents (a much simpler baseline), which is not tested as an ablation/baseline in the comparison table.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem framing: the paper convincingly distinguishes multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing from single-agent hallucination and from purely textual hallucination snowballing, and grounds this distinction in detailed turn-, layer-, and token-wise attention analyses.

The identification of a small subset of 'unimodal' vision tokens in middle layers that are disproportionately important for preserving visual evidence is an interesting and non-obvious empirical finding, well supported by systematic token-dropping ablations across multiple layers and token-selection criteria.

Extremely thorough experimental validation: 10 base VLMs (7B-34B), 4 MAS structures, 8 comprehensive/hallucination benchmarks plus 4 augmented multi-image/video benchmarks, 5 competing single-agent hallucination-mitigation baselines re-purposed for MAS, ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity studies, efficiency/latency analysis, and qualitative case studies.

Proposes a quantitative Hallucination Snowballing (HS) metric that explicitly captures both severity and propagation distance, enabling more direct measurement of the phenomenon than standard single-turn metrics.

Provides a practical Key-Norm-based alternative to attention-score-based token selection for compatibility with Flash-Attention, showing the method's applicability to modern efficient-inference settings.

Consistent, non-trivial improvements are shown across essentially all tested settings, including scaling to larger models (13B-34B) and different MAS topologies, with reasonable computational overhead (single-digit to low double-digit percentage increases in latency/FLOPs).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution (selecting a subset of informative vision tokens to relay across turns + reweighting attention via temperature scaling and score reallocation) is a fairly direct combination of existing ideas from token pruning/selection and attention-steering literature, applied to a new setting rather than being a fundamentally new mechanism.

Despite being described as 'lightweight' and 'model-agnostic', ViF requires a two-stage training pipeline (pre-training + instruction tuning) for the transformer block that contextualizes relay tokens; details of the training data used for this pipeline are not clearly specified, which weakens the plug-and-play claim and reproducibility.

The four 'MAS structures' tested differ only in inter-agent connection topology while the underlying dual-agent actor-critic interaction protocol is held fixed; this narrows the claim of generality across genuinely different multi-agent collaboration paradigms (e.g., debate, voting, hierarchical planning with distinct roles).

The proposed HS metric depends on an LLM judge (GPT-5) for hallucination severity scoring, which introduces potential circularity/bias and limited transparency (no inter-rater reliability beyond a single cross-check with Gemini 2.5 Pro on one benchmark).

Several hyperparameters (ω, τ, α1, α2) are tuned and appear sensitive to benchmark-specific optimal values (Tables 12-14), raising concerns about overfitting to the evaluated benchmarks and how well these values transfer to unseen tasks/domains.
No error bars, variance, or multiple-run statistics are reported for the main results, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported 1-3 point average improvements.
The claim that larger models 'possess stronger latent potential unlocked by ViF' is speculative and not directly tested with a controlled analysis isolating model capacity from other confounds.
